Homeostasis.intro: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment. It ensures cells can function correctly despite changes in conditions.

sections.title: What is Homeostasis?
points: Control of internal conditions: body temperature (37°C), blood glucose, water content
Uses negative feedback — when conditions change, the response corrects them back to the set point

callout.label: Key Concept
callout.text: Negative feedback always returns conditions BACK to the normal level. Response always OPPOSES the original change.

keyTerms.def: Maintenance of a stable internal environment
A control mechanism where the response reverses the original change
A muscle or gland that brings about a response

examTips: Negative feedback always returns to the set point — the response opposes the change.
Examples: temperature, blood glucose, water balance.
commonMistakes: Confusing negative feedback (corrects) with positive feedback (amplifies).
clozePassages: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite changes in external conditions. The body regulates blood glucose concentration, body temperature, and water content. These are controlled by negative feedback mechanisms — when a condition moves away from its set point, receptors detect this and effectors bring it back. Examples include sweating to cool down and shivering to warm up.

Negative feedback is the mechanism used in homeostasis to keep conditions within a narrow range. When a variable deviates from its set point, receptors detect the change and send signals to a control centre. The control centre sends instructions to effectors such as muscles or glands to counteract the change. This brings the variable back to the set point, completing the feedback loop.

The body regulates temperature through several mechanisms. When too hot, sweat glands produce sweat which cools the skin as it evaporates. Vasodilation occurs — blood vessels near the skin surface widen, allowing more heat to radiate away. When too cold, vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to the skin. Shivering occurs — rapid muscle contractions generate heat. All these responses are controlled by the hypothalamus.

Nervous System.intro: The nervous system allows rapid detection and response to changes. It consists of the CNS (brain and spinal cord) and peripheral nerves.

sections.title: Structure
points: Sensory neurones — from receptors TO CNS
Motor neurones — from CNS TO effectors
Relay neurones — connect in CNS

callout.label: Why Reflexes Are Fast
callout.text: Reflexes bypass the brain — coordinated in spinal cord. Pupil reflex, withdrawal reflex.

keyTerms.def: Gap between neurones — neurotransmitters carry signal across
Pathway of neurones in a reflex action

examTips: Reflexes bypass the brain — faster response.
Sensory = TO CNS. Motor = FROM CNS.
commonMistakes: Saying reflexes involve conscious thought — they do not.
clozePassages: The nervous system detects and responds to changes in the environment. Receptors in sense organs detect stimuli. Electrical impulses travel along sensory neurones to the brain or spinal cord. The brain processes the information and sends impulses along motor neurones to effectors such as muscles or glands, which produce a response. This pathway is called a stimulus-response pathway.

A reflex arc is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought. The pathway goes: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone in spinal cord → motor neurone → effector → response. Reflexes are faster than voluntary responses because they bypass the brain. Examples include the knee-jerk reflex and withdrawing your hand from a hot object.

Synapses are junctions between neurones. When an electrical impulse reaches a synapse, neurotransmitters are released into the synaptic gap. These chemicals diffuse across and bind to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse. Drugs and toxins can affect synaptic transmission — for example, some drugs block neurotransmitter receptors or prevent their reuptake.

Hormones.intro: Hormones are chemical messengers produced by glands, carried in blood to target organs. Slower and longer-lasting than nervous responses.

sections.title: Nervous vs Hormonal
points: Nervous: fast, short-lived, electrical, specific pathway
Hormonal: slower, longer-lasting, chemical, bloodstream

sections.title: Key Hormones
points: Adrenaline — adrenal glands; fight or flight; increases heart rate
Insulin — pancreas; lowers blood glucose
Glucagon — pancreas; raises blood glucose
Oestrogen — ovaries; female puberty, menstrual cycle
Testosterone — testes; male puberty

keyTerms.def: Chemical messenger carried in blood to target organs
Fight or flight hormone from adrenal glands
Organ that responds to a specific hormone

examTips: Hormones travel in blood — reach all organs but only affect targets.
Hormonal = slow and long-lasting; Nervous = fast and short.
commonMistakes: Confusing slow hormonal with fast nervous responses.
clozePassages: Hormones are chemical messengers produced by endocrine glands and released into the bloodstream. They travel to target organs where they produce a response. Hormonal responses are slower but longer-lasting than nervous responses. Key endocrine glands include the pituitary gland (the master gland), thyroid, adrenal glands, pancreas, and reproductive organs.

The menstrual cycle is controlled by several hormones. FSH (follicle stimulating hormone) from the pituitary gland stimulates an egg to develop. Oestrogen from the ovaries causes the uterus lining to thicken. LH (luteinising hormone) triggers ovulation. Progesterone maintains the uterine lining after ovulation. If fertilisation does not occur, hormone levels fall and menstruation begins.

Hormonal contraception works by preventing ovulation or fertilisation. The contraceptive pill contains oestrogen and progesterone which inhibit FSH production, preventing eggs from maturing. Progesterone-only pills thicken cervical mucus to prevent sperm entry. IUDs prevent implantation of fertilised eggs. Hormonal contraceptives are highly effective but do not protect against sexually transmitted infections.

Blood Glucose.intro: Blood glucose must be kept within a narrow range. Insulin and glucagon work together as a negative feedback pair to achieve this.

sections.title: Regulation
points: High glucose → pancreas releases INSULIN → glucose → glycogen in liver → glucose falls
Low glucose → pancreas releases GLUCAGON → glycogen → glucose in liver → glucose rises

callout.label: Negative Feedback Pair
callout.text: Insulin lowers glucose. Glucagon raises glucose. They are antagonistic hormones.

sections.title: Diabetes
points: Type 1 — pancreas makes no insulin; autoimmune; treated with insulin injections
Type 2 — cells don't respond to insulin; linked to obesity; managed by diet/exercise/medication

keyTerms.def: Lowers blood glucose — stimulates glycogen storage
Raises blood glucose — stimulates glycogen breakdown
Storage form of glucose in liver and muscles
Pancreas produces no insulin — requires injections
Cells resistant to insulin — linked to lifestyle

examTips: Insulin = stores glucose as glycogen. Glucagon = releases glucose from glycogen.
Type 1 treated with insulin; Type 2 often managed with lifestyle changes.
commonMistakes: Forgetting glycogen is stored in LIVER and muscles.
clozePassages: Blood glucose concentration is regulated by the pancreas. After a meal, blood glucose rises. The pancreas releases insulin, which causes cells to take up glucose from the blood. Excess glucose is converted to glycogen and stored in the liver and muscles. When blood glucose falls too low, the pancreas releases glucagon, which stimulates the liver to convert glycogen back to glucose.

Type 1 diabetes is caused by the immune system destroying the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas. Sufferers must inject insulin daily to regulate blood glucose. Type 2 diabetes occurs when cells become less responsive to insulin. It is linked to obesity and can often be managed through diet and exercise. Without treatment, high blood glucose causes damage to blood vessels and nerves.

Glucagon and insulin work antagonistically to regulate blood glucose levels — this is an example of negative feedback. When glucose is too high, insulin is released and glucose is removed from the blood. When glucose is too low, glucagon is released and glucose is added to the blood. This keeps blood glucose within a narrow range, ensuring cells always have enough glucose for respiration.

Reproduction.intro: Reproduction is controlled by hormones. The menstrual cycle involves four key hormones, and fertility can be controlled using synthetic hormones.

sections.title: The Menstrual Cycle
points: FSH (pituitary) — stimulates egg maturation; stimulates oestrogen
Oestrogen (ovary) — repairs uterus lining; inhibits FSH; stimulates LH surge
LH (pituitary) — triggers ovulation at day 14
Progesterone (corpus luteum) — maintains uterus lining; inhibits FSH and LH

sections.title: Contraception
points: Pill — contains oestrogen/progesterone; inhibits FSH; prevents ovulation
Implant/injection — long-acting progesterone
Barrier methods (condoms, diaphragm) — not hormonal

sections.title: IVF
points: FSH and LH given to stimulate multiple egg production
Eggs collected and fertilised with sperm outside body
Embryo(s) implanted into uterus
Low success rate; emotional strain; ethical issues with unused embryos

keyTerms.def: Rebuilds uterus lining; triggers LH surge
In vitro fertilisation — fertilisation outside the body

examTips: FSH stimulates oestrogen; oestrogen inhibits FSH (negative feedback).
IVF uses FSH to stimulate multiple egg production.
Know pros and cons of IVF for evaluate questions.
commonMistakes: Confusing FSH (egg maturation) with LH (ovulation trigger).
Forgetting oestrogen inhibits FSH — this is the negative feedback.
clozePassages: Puberty is triggered by the release of sex hormones. In males, testosterone from the testes stimulates sperm production and the development of secondary sexual characteristics. In females, oestrogen from the ovaries stimulates egg maturation and secondary sexual characteristics. Puberty in females also involves the beginning of the menstrual cycle. The pituitary gland controls the release of these sex hormones.

IVF (in vitro fertilisation) is a fertility treatment used when natural conception is not possible. The woman is given FSH and LH to stimulate multiple eggs to mature. Eggs are collected and fertilised with sperm outside the body. The resulting embryos are checked for genetic disorders if required, then one or two are placed in the uterus. IVF has a relatively low success rate and raises ethical questions about unused embryos.

Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of a male gamete (sperm) and female gamete (egg) at fertilisation. The resulting zygote has a unique combination of genetic material from both parents, producing variation. Asexual reproduction involves only one parent and produces genetically identical offspring called clones. Plants such as strawberries reproduce asexually by sending out runners. Asexual reproduction is faster but produces no genetic variation.
